security_spec.violation_condition: In QEMU pmp_hart_has_privs() at pmp.c:435, an M-mode access matching a PMP entry with L bit clear returns success with full R/W/X permissions regardless of the entry's R/W/X bits. The spec clarification states the 'If the L bit is clear and the privilege mode of the access is M, the access succeeds' rule does NOT supersede the priority-and-matching rule: an access that is partially matched (spans a PMP boundary) must fail even for M-mode to an unlocked region. QEMU correctly enforces partial-match failures (pmp.c:413-418) before checking the L bit, but the sequential logic at lines 424-517 must ensure that once a PMP entry matches all bytes, the L-cleared M-mode bypass at line 435 does not incorrectly override the all-bytes-matching requirement for accesses crossing into regions with different PMP entries.
security_spec.summary: QEMU must ensure M-mode access to unlocked PMP regions correctly fails for partially-matching accesses spanning PMP boundaries; the spec clarification confirms the priority/matching-all-bytes rule takes precedence over the M-mode unlocked bypass.

findings.finding: The PMP priority-and-matching logic correctly enforces the spec's ordering requirements. Partial-match checks (lines 413-418: s+e==1) execute BEFORE the L-cleared M-mode bypass (lines 434-437), so boundary-crossing accesses always fail irrespective of privilege mode or L-bit state. The loop iterates from lowest-numbered entry to highest (the priority order mandated by norm:pmp_entry_priority), and the first matching entry (either partial or full) determines the outcome. A partial match at any priority level immediately returns false with allowed_privs=0, correctly implementing norm:pmp_full_match_required.

spec_citations.excerpt: PMP entries are statically prioritized. The lowest-numbered PMP entry that matches any byte of a memory operation determines whether that operation succeeds or fails. The matching PMP entry must match all bytes of a memory operation, or the operation fails, irrespective of the L, R, W, and X bits.

When the L bit is set, these permissions are enforced for all privilege modes. When the L bit is clear, any M-mode access matching the PMP entry will succeed; the R/W/X permissions apply only to S and U modes.

If a PMP entry matches all bytes of a memory operation, then the L, R, W, and X bits determine whether the operation succeeds or fails. If the L bit is clear and the privilege mode of the access is M, the operation succeeds.

findings.finding: The standard PMP privilege check at lines 434-437 correctly implements the spec's L-bit M-mode behavior: M-mode accesses to unlocked regions (L=0) succeed with full R/W/X permissions regardless of the entry's R/W/X bits, while locked regions (L=1) and non-M-mode accesses are gated by the cfg_reg R/W/X bits. The allowed_privs mask is initialized to P READ|WRITE|EXEC (0x07), so the logical-AND with cfg_reg only extracts bits 0-2 (R/W/X). The L bit at position 7 and A field at positions 3-4 in cfg_reg do not interfere with the permission check.

spec_citations.excerpt: When the L bit is set, these permissions are enforced for all privilege modes. When the L bit is clear, any M-mode access matching the PMP entry will succeed; the R/W/X permissions apply only to S and U modes.

findings.finding: The partial-match enforcement at lines 413-418 correctly captures the norm:pmp_full_match_required rule. When s+e==1 (the start and end addresses of the access are not both in or both out of the PMP entry), the function immediately returns false with allowed_privs=0. This runs before any privilege-mode or L-bit check, so M-mode accesses crossing PMP boundaries always fail. This logic correctly handles the scenario described in the spec example: an 8-byte access to 0x8-0xF spanning a 4-byte entry at 0xC-0xF will be detected as partially matching that entry and will fail.

spec_citations.excerpt: The matching PMP entry must match all bytes of a memory operation, or the operation fails, irrespective of the L, R, W, and X bits. For example, if a PMP entry is configured to match the four-byte range 0xC-0xF, then an 8-byte access to the range 0x8-0xF will fail, assuming that PMP entry is the highest-priority entry that matches those addresses.

findings.finding: The Smepmp (MML=1) privilege check at lines 438-509 correctly implements the Smepmp truth table from the spec. The pmp_get_smepmp_operation() function extracts a 4-bit operation code from cfg_reg bits: ((L>>4) | (R<<2) | W | (X>>2)). The M-mode switch (lines 446-475) and S/U-mode switch (lines 476-508) map all 16 possible operation codes to the correct allowed_privs values per the Smepmp spec truth table. For example: operation 0 (LRWX=0000) → allowed_privs=0 for both M and S/U (inaccessible); operation 2 (LRWX=0010) → PMP_READ|PMP_WRITE for M, PMP_READ for S/U (shared data, read/write on M, read-only on S/U); operation 9 (LRWX=1001) → PMP_EXEC for M, 0 for S/U (locked execute-only).

spec_citations.excerpt: The physical memory protection rules when mseccfg.MML is set to 1 are summarized in the truth table below. [columns: L|R|W|X, M Mode, S/U Mode] ... 0|0|0|0 → Inaccessible region ... 0|0|1|0 → Shared data region: Read/write on M mode, read-only on S/U mode ... 1|0|0|1 → Locked Execute-only region, Access Exception for S/U

When mseccfg.MML is set: The meaning of pmpcfg.L changes: Instead of marking a rule as locked and enforced in all modes, it now marks a rule as M-mode-only when set and S/U-mode-only when unset. An M-mode-only rule is enforced on Machine mode and denied in Supervisor or User mode. An S/U-mode-only rule is enforced on Supervisor and User modes and denied on Machine mode.

findings.finding: PMP entries with A=OFF are correctly skipped during address-matching. Line 424 checks '(PMP_AMATCH_OFF != a_field)' before entering the privilege check block, so disabled PMP entries (A=OFF) never participate in address matching. This is correct because A=OFF entries have sa=0, ea=-1 (matching all addresses) but are not valid PMP rules per the spec definition. If A=OFF entries were not skipped, they would match every access and block lower-priority entries from ever being evaluated.

spec_citations.excerpt: If at least one PMP entry is implemented, but all PMP entries' A fields are set to OFF, then all S-mode and U-mode memory accesses will fail.

findings.finding: The default (no-match) privilege logic correctly handles all spec-mandated cases: (1) MMWP set → deny all including M-mode; (2) MML set → M-mode allowed only for non-execute accesses (READ|WRITE), others denied; (3) Standard PMP: M-mode or no PMP implemented → full access, S/U-mode with any PMP rules → denied. This correctly implements norms pmp_no_entry_match (M-mode access succeeds when no entry matches), mseccfg_mmwp_op (default deny for M-mode when MMWP set), and mseccfg_mml_exec_code (M-mode code execution restricted under MML).

spec_citations.excerpt: If no PMP entry matches an M-mode memory operation, the operation succeeds. If no PMP entry matches an S-mode or U-mode memory operation, but at least one PMP entry is implemented, the operation fails.
When [mseccfg.MMWP] is set it changes the default PMP policy for M-mode when accessing memory regions that don't have a matching PMP rule, to denied instead of ignored.
Executing code with Machine mode privileges is only possible from memory regions with a matching M-mode-only rule or a locked Shared-Region rule with executable privileges.

findings.finding: CSR write to pmpcfg correctly triggers TLB flush when any PMP configuration is modified. The function iterates through all 4 or 8 configurations in the CSR (depending on MXL), applies each via pmp_write_cfg which validates locks, Smepmp restrictions, and PMP_MTMATCH. On any modification (modified=true), it calls pmp_update_rule_nums() to recount active rules and tlb_flush() to invalidate all TLB entries. This correctly implements the norm:pmp_sfence_required rule that PMP changes must synchronize with the virtual memory system via SFENCE.VMA — in QEMU's software TLB model, tlb_flush() is the equivalent of the hardware SFENCE.VMA required by the spec.

spec_citations.excerpt: when the PMP settings are modified, M-mode software must synchronize the PMP settings with the virtual memory system and any PMP or address-translation caches. This is accomplished by executing an SFENCE.VMA instruction with rs1=x0 and rs2=x0, after the PMP CSRs are written.

findings.finding: CSR write to pmpaddr correctly validates lock bits, including the TOR dependency where entry i's lock state also affects writes to pmpaddr[i-1] (lines 591-599). On modification, pmp_update_rule_addr recalculates SA/EA for the affected entry (and the next entry if it uses TOR), and tlb_flush synchronizes the TLB. The validation ensures that writes to locked entries are silently ignored per norm:pmp_l_bit_function and norm:pmp_l_bit_write_protection.

spec_citations.excerpt: The L bit indicates that the PMP entry is locked, i.e., writes to the configuration register and associated address registers are ignored. If PMP entry i is locked, writes to pmpicfg and pmpaddri are ignored. Additionally, if PMP entry i is locked and pmpicfg.A is set to TOR, writes to pmpaddri-1 are ignored.

findings.finding: mseccfg CSR write correctly implements sticky-bit semantics for MMWP and MML fields (once set, cannot be cleared until PMP reset), and the RLB re-lock prevention (RLB cannot be set if any PMP entries are locked). When MMWP or MML state changes, tlb_flush is triggered. Lines 686-688: the existing sticky bits value is preserved by OR-ing them back into the new value, and any change in sticky bit state triggers a TLB flush. This matches the norm:mseccfg_mmwp_op_warl (MMWP is sticky, reset to 0 only on PMP reset) and norm:mseccfg_mml_sticky (MML is sticky) rules.

spec_citations.excerpt: The mseccfg.MMWP is a WARL field. This is a sticky bit, meaning that once set it cannot be unset until a PMP reset.
The mseccfg.MML is a WARL field. This is a sticky bit, meaning that once set it cannot be unset until a PMP reset.

findings.finding: PMP state is correctly included in the VMState migration structure. The vmstate_pmp_entry records both addr_reg (UINTTL) and cfg_reg (UINT8) for each PMP entry. The vmstate_pmp uses pmp_needed() to conditionally include PMP state only when PMP is configured, and pmp_post_load() to recalculate SA/EA addresses and rule counts after migration. This ensures that PMP settings survive live migration correctly, preventing silent privilege escalation that would occur if PMP state were lost during migration.

spec_citations.excerpt: Locked PMP entries remain locked until the hart is reset.
